unique.citation: Shahid NF. When Average Calibration Fails: Site-Conditional Federated Conformal Risk Control. arXiv preprint (v1 18 Jun 2026, v3 24 Jul 2026); arXiv comment: 'Submitted to the DeCaF Workshop at MICCAI 2026'.
unique.what_it_does: Uses FeTS-2022 brain-tumour data (1,251 subjects, 20 institutions). A single pooled conformal-risk-control threshold misses the FNR target at 40% of sites. The paper proposes 'risk-curve shrinkage': R_k^shrink(lambda) = w_k*R_k(lambda) + (1-w_k)*R_global(lambda) + corr_k, with w_k = n_k/(n_k+n0). The paper calls this 'the standard empirical Bayes form where n0 acts as prior precision'. n0 is picked by leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis (n0=19 gives 2.7/20 violating sites at a 2.0x stretch). Results are reported per site (violation counts, worst-site FNR).
unique.difference_to_HSC: The mechanism is essentially HSC's: one pseudo-count weight n/(n+n0) mixes a unit's own calibration curve with a pooled curve (for coverage, a risk curve is 1 minus the score CDF). It also uses leave-one-unit-out tuning and per-unit evaluation. Differences: (1) it is conformal risk control for segmentation FNR, not regression intervals. (2) The units are existing sites with fixed calibration sets; the paper does not address a new site joining with few samples. (3) The prior is the sample-size-weighted global pool, with no similarity (kNN) prior and no stage matching. This fits HSC's own ablation finding that shrinkage, not the prior, is the active ingredient. (4) It adds an ad hoc correction term, the paper calls it 'a heuristic interpolation', there is no guarantee, and n0 is chosen on the same test partitions. It is a workshop preprint. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
unique.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; arXiv abs page (versions/comments); arXiv HTML full text v3 read via WebFetch (Eq. 2, weight definition, LOSO selection, per-site metrics)

unique.citation: Mallick S, Tchetgen Tchetgen E, Dobriban E, Lee Y. Generalized Hierarchical Conformal Prediction. arXiv preprint, 16 Aug 2026 (stat.ME).
unique.what_it_does: Covers prediction for a group after a few (o) of its observations are already collected. Standard hierarchical conformal prediction (HCP) cannot use these, and within-group conformal is uninformative at small o. GHCP restores exchangeability by giving the test group a randomly 'donated' group size. It splits the o observations: floor(o/2) fit a local predictor that is shrunk toward the global one (lambda = floor(o/2)/(|S_train|+floor(o/2))). The rest are held-out scores, pooled with the reference groups' scores in one weighted empirical distribution (Eq. 5). Each reference group gets total weight 1/(|S_cal|+1); the test group gets the same share, with its unobserved part placed at +infinity. Theorem 2.1 proves a finite-sample marginal guarantee. A restricted-donor variant is included. Evaluation uses simulations and the American Community Survey with o in {0,5,10,15,20}.
unique.difference_to_HSC: Same problem as HSC: a new unit with a few of its own observations, whose own scores are pooled with population scores. GHCP has a finite-sample marginal guarantee; HSC has none. In GHCP the test group's own scores never weigh more than one group's share (1/(K+1)). In HSC the own-score weight n_b/(kappa+n_b+1) grows until the own scores dominate. GHCP has no tuned kappa, no similarity prior and no stage matching. It shrinks the predictor rather than the score CDF, uses unnormalised absolute residuals, and treats o as fixed rather than a growing sequence; there is no time series. Only marginal coverage is reported; I saw no per-group coverage distribution, but the appendix was not fully read. This is the principled counterpart HSC should discuss, and ideally run as a baseline. Not cited in manuscript/references.py; its predecessor Lee et al. 2023 (lee2023hier) is cited.
unique.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; arXiv abs page; arXiv HTML full text v1 read via WebFetch (Eq. 3 and 5, Theorem 2.1, experimental settings). The last ~106k characters were not read.

unique.citation: Rafe A, Das S. Socio-Conformal Calibration in Complex Survey Data: Marginal Validity Is Not Enough for Subgroup Reliability. arXiv preprint, 7 May 2026.
unique.what_it_does: Ordinal conformal prediction on the Pew American Trends Panel (Wave 152; n=4,591; 12 race x education subgroups) over 100 respondent-disjoint splits. It compares split conformal, Mondrian, and a 'regularized Mondrian' comparator: q_g^reg = w_g*q_g + (1-w_g)*q_global, with w_g = n_g/(n_g+lambda) and lambda = 50 fixed. The comparator is motivated by James-Stein shrinkage and 'partial pooling in hierarchical models'. The authors call it 'an empirical comparator, not a theorem-backed contribution'. It reduces threshold instability but gives no decisive fairness gain. The main metric is the survey-weighted subgroup coverage gap.
unique.difference_to_HSC: Same n/(n+lambda) shrinkage toward a pooled calibration, but applied to quantile thresholds rather than score CDFs. lambda is fixed rather than tuned leave-one-building-out. The groups are static demographic cells, not new units accumulating data; the prior is global with no neighbour prior; the task is classification sets. The neutral or negative result contrasts with HSC's gains and shows the benefit of shrinkage depends on the setting. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
unique.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; arXiv HTML full text read via WebFetch (Eq. 4, Appendix B on lambda); first surfaced by a WebSearch for empirical-Bayes Mondrian shrinkage

unique.citation: Lin Z, Trivedi S, Sun J. Conformal Prediction with Temporal Quantile Adjustments. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022), pp. 31017-31030.
unique.what_it_does: Prediction intervals for cross-sectional time series (for example, patients). The split-conformal quantile is taken over other series' scores at the same time step. TQA adjusts the queried quantile for each series using its own past: TQA-B predicts a rank from an exponentially decayed mean of the series' own residuals; TQA-E uses an ACI-like update delta <- delta + gamma*(err - alpha) on the series' own miscoverages. The paper separates cross-sectional from longitudinal (per-series) coverage. It reports 'tail coverage' = average coverage of the least-covered 10% of series.
unique.difference_to_HSC: Same evaluation lens: per-unit (longitudinal) coverage and its lower tail, close in spirit to HSC's P10 coverage and share of buildings under 0.85. Also the same structure of population calibration plus the unit's own history. TQA moves the quantile level instead of mixing population and own score distributions with a pseudo-count, and has no similarity prior or onboarding-stage indexing. Its data are health, insurance, COVID, EEG and GEFCom2014 load (days as units). TQA-E is close to HSC's ACI baseline; TQA-B would be a distinct, relevant baseline. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
unique.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; WebSearch result giving the NeurIPS 2022 proceedings entry and pages; ar5iv full text read via WebFetch (TQA-B/TQA-E definitions, tail-coverage metric, datasets)

unique.citation: Lin Z, Trivedi S, Sun J. Conformal Prediction Intervals with Temporal Dependence. Transactions on Machine Learning Research (September 2022), per the arXiv comments field.
unique.what_it_does: Defines cross-sectional and longitudinal validity for time-series regression across a cross-section, and shows distribution-free longitudinal validity is theoretically impossible. CPTD keeps strict cross-sectional validity while improving longitudinal coverage. The test series S_{N+1} is a new unit, exchangeable with the calibration series. Scores are normalised by the series' own past mean absolute residual (CPTD-M) or by a rank-based normaliser (CPTD-R). In CPTD-R a 'prior' rank-percentile of 0.5 'has the same weight as any actual observation'. The interval comes from the cross-sectional quantile of these normalised scores. The metric is mean coverage of the least-covered 10% of series.
unique.difference_to_HSC: Same evaluation (per-series coverage of new series calibrated on other series), and the impossibility result bounds what HSC can claim per building. The mechanism is related: population calibration of scores normalised by the unit's own history, plus a one-pseudo-observation prior on the rank. HSC instead normalises by mean load and mixes score CDFs with a tuned kappa and a neighbour prior. CPTD is not stage-indexed and its load data is the GEFCom2014 single series with days as units. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
unique.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; arXiv abs page comments (TMLR Sept 2022); ar5iv full text read via WebFetch (CPTD-M/R, prior weight, tail coverage, datasets)

unique.citation: Zhang Z, Lu Z, Yang H. The Benefit of Being Bayesian in Online Conformal Prediction. arXiv preprint (v1 Oct 2024, v2 May 2025).
unique.what_it_does: Online conformal prediction that keeps a belief over the score distribution, regularised by a prior: P_t = lambda_t*P_0 + (1-lambda_t)*empirical distribution of past scores. The paper links this to a Dirichlet-process posterior mean with lambda = alpha/(alpha+n). P_0 is an arbitrary distribution on [0,R], uniform in the main analysis; the theory uses lambda_t = 1/sqrt(t). One belief serves several confidence levels; regret bounds hold in the adversarial case and correct coverage when data are iid.
unique.difference_to_HSC: The functional form is the same as HSC's mixture F = (kappa*F_prior + #{e_i<=e})/(kappa+n_b+1): a DP-posterior-mean or prior-regularised empirical belief. The difference is the prior: here it is a fixed uninformative distribution, not learned from similar units or matched by stage. There is a single sequence with no population or new-unit structure, and lambda_t follows a theoretical schedule rather than leave-one-building-out tuning. HSC should acknowledge its update as this Bayesian-regularised empirical belief and cite this as the online-conformal precedent. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
unique.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract (from a title query for 'Bayesian' AND 'conformal'); arXiv HTML v2 read via WebFetch (Eq. 6 belief form, DP link, prior choice)

unique.citation: Dunn R, Wasserman L, Ramdas A. Distribution-Free Prediction Sets for Two-Layer Hierarchical Models. Journal of the American Statistical Association 2023;118(544):2491-2502.
unique.what_it_does: Conformal methods for grouped data. CDF pooling is an equal-weight average of the groups' empirical CDFs, with coverage only asymptotic as k grows. Single and repeated subsampling give finite-sample guarantees. Task 1 predicts for a new group. Task 2 predicts a new observation for an existing subject, using a James-Stein shrinkage estimate of that subject's mean in the nonconformity score (finite-sample guarantee from within-subject conformal, non-trivial only if n1 > 1/alpha - 1). The paper states 'supervised conformal methods that borrow strength across subjects to construct prediction sets for an existing subject remain an open problem.'
unique.difference_to_HSC: HSC's F_prior is a CDF pooling restricted to K neighbour buildings. HSC's problem is Task 2 in a supervised, sequential setting, which is the open problem Dunn et al. name, and that sentence is a good positioning hook. Dunn et al. shrink the location, not the score distribution, and have no time series. Already cited in the manuscript (key dunn2023).
unique.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; ar5iv full text read via WebFetch (CDF pooling definition, Task 2 shrinkage formula, 'open problem' quote); WebSearch result giving the JASA volume, pages and DOI

unique.citation: Ding T, Fermanian J-B, Salmon J. Conformal Prediction for Long-Tailed Classification. arXiv preprint (v1 Jul 2025; v3 revised 26 Feb 2026).
unique.what_it_does: Interp-Q interpolates between class-wise and marginal conformal thresholds: q_y = tau*q_y^CW + (1-tau)*q_hat. A single tau is used for every class, and marginal coverage is at least 1-2*alpha. Fuzzy Classwise CP pools calibration scores across classes with kernel weights on a class embedding (default based on training prevalence), then reconformalises for 1-alpha marginal coverage. The paper also adds a prevalence-adjusted softmax score that targets macro-coverage.
unique.difference_to_HSC: Its two devices match HSC's two ingredients: interpolating between group-specific and pooled calibration, and similarity-kernel borrowing from other groups. But tau does not depend on a group's sample size, whereas HSC's own-score weight grows with n_b. Classes are not new units accumulating data, the task is classification, and there is no time series or onboarding. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
unique.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; arXiv HTML v3 read via WebFetch (Interp-Q formula, Fuzzy CP weights, guarantees)

unique.citation: Ding T, Angelopoulos AN, Bates S, Jordan MI, Tibshirani RJ. Class-Conditional Conformal Prediction with Many Classes. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023).

unique.citation: Bersson E, Hoff PD. Optimal Conformal Prediction for Small Areas. Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology 2024;12(5):1464-1488.
unique.what_it_does: Builds an area-level prediction region for a future observation with guaranteed area-level frequentist coverage. The conformity measure is the posterior predictive density of a working model that brings in indirect information from other areas. The region is valid whatever the working model, and has minimum expected volume if the working model is correct. Under a normal working model it is an interval. Applied to EPA radon survey data.
unique.difference_to_HSC: Borrows strength across units through the conformity score while keeping calibration within each area, which preserves exact per-area coverage. HSC borrows in the calibration distribution, which helps when n_b is tiny but gives up exact per-unit validity. A reviewer may raise it as the alternative design. No time series and no new-unit onboarding. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.

unique.citation: Bashari M, Lotan RM, Lee Y, Dobriban E, Romano Y. Synthetic-Powered Predictive Inference. arXiv preprint, 19 May 2025.
unique.what_it_does: SPI adds synthetic or auxiliary data to a scarce real calibration set. A 'score transporter', an empirical quantile mapping, aligns the trusted real scores with the synthetic scores. It achieves finite-sample coverage without assumptions about the synthetic distribution, and gives much tighter sets when the two score distributions are well aligned.
unique.difference_to_HSC: A principled counterpart to HSC's 'small own score set plus large auxiliary pool' mixture: neighbour-building scores would play the role of the synthetic scores. SPI keeps a finite-sample guarantee; HSC's convex CDF mixture with tuned kappa has none. SPI does not work per unit or sequentially. The follow-up GESPI (arXiv:2509.20345) adaptively falls back to real data only when the auxiliary data are poor. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.

unique.citation: Octadion O, Yudistira N, Nakashima Y. Predicted Class Correction: Conformal Thresholds for Classes with No Calibration Data. arXiv preprint, 18 Oct 2026.
unique.what_it_does: PCC regresses the offset between per-class and marginal conformal quantiles on label-free descriptors of the classifier head. It shrinks the predicted offset by one scalar chosen on the labelled classes, then refits a single marginal offset, so the marginal guarantee is kept. This gives classes with zero calibration examples their own thresholds and improves worst-class coverage on ImageNet. It also notes that below about 35 test examples per class, worst-class coverage 'becomes unmeasurable before it becomes unachievable'.
unique.difference_to_HSC: Similar to HSC's descriptor-based prior for units with no own data (descriptor to expected calibration level), with shrinkage tuned on other units. PCC predicts a threshold offset by regression instead of pooling neighbour CDFs, and has no accumulation of own scores and no time series. Its evaluation caveat applies to HSC's per-building coverage over 56 days: few target days make per-unit coverage noisy. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.

unique.citation: Batra D, Mercuri S, Khraishi R. Conformal Predictions for Longitudinal Data. arXiv preprint, 4 Oct 2023.
unique.what_it_does: LPCI is a conformal method for longitudinal (panel) data that targets both cross-sectional and longitudinal coverage without infinitely wide intervals. It models the residuals as a quantile fixed-effects regression, a quantile regressor with unit effects, and proves asymptotic coverage in both dimensions.

LPCI pools through a quantile regression with unit fixed effects, which needs residual history for each unit, rather than a pseudo-count mixture with a neighbour prior for new units. Guarantees are asymptotic, and there is no onboarding-stage evaluation. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.

unique.citation: Jeon, Byung-ki (2026). coldstart-conformal-solar: analysis code for auditing cold-start conformal prediction intervals of solar irradiance forecasts at unseen stations (v1.2). Zenodo code record, published 2026-11-06. It accompanies the manuscript "A two-network audit shows when conformal prediction intervals for solar irradiance forecasts remain valid at newly commissioned stations" (Scientific Reports, under review, second revision).
unique.identifier: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24002627 (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24002626; only one version listed)
unique.what_it_does: A leave-one-station-out audit of conformal intervals for short-term solar irradiance (GHI) forecasts at a newly commissioned station with no local calibration data. It covers 13 NOAA SURFRAD/SOLRAD stations and 28 PV-Live stations, four base forecasters (including gradient-boosted QR and a multi-quantile NN), horizons from 15 min to 6 h, and nominal levels 80/90/95%. It uses CQR scores max(lo-y, y-hi). It compares eight calibration strategies: raw quantiles; pooled donors; distance-weighted donors; Wasserstein-weighted donors; selected/nearest donors; local-only windows of 1-182 days; a donor+local mixture; delayed-feedback ACI seeded with donor scores; and a full-local-year oracle. It also estimates a 'calibration-budget law' B* (days of local data needed for coverage within 1 pp) and a prospective self-certification rule. In the released code (src/run_cp_matrix.py, src/cp_core.py), the mixture M4_mix gives the donor scores a total mass m (main 150, sensitivity 50 and 400) and each local score weight 1, then takes a weighted CP quantile with test weight 1: Q = inf{q : m*F_donor(q) + #{local <= q} >= (1-alpha)(m + n_local + 1)}. The bundled results digest (NUMBERS.md) shows the mixture beating local-only on Winkler score at budgets of 1, 5 and 21 days, with the gap vanishing by about 91 days. It also shows donor similarity (distance, kt-Wasserstein) not predicting donor suitability: within-fold Spearman rho is about 0, and nearest-donor and pooled give similar shares of stations within 2 pp.
unique.difference_to_HSC: The mixture formula is algebraically the same as HSC's, with kappa = m. Their m is fixed a priori with a sensitivity grid; it is not chosen by leave-one-unit-out. The domain is solar irradiance at 41 stations, not building or customer load at 842 buildings and 315 clients. Donors are pooled or weighted by geographic or kt distance, not kNN in a load-shape descriptor, and there is no stage-matched prior. Normalisation is clear-sky, not by mean load. The work is not yet peer-reviewed. The record has been public only since 6 Nov 2026, so the two are nearly simultaneous, but the code files carry 1-2 Aug 2026 timestamps. Its finding that similarity weighting does not help matches HSC's null kNN-prior ablation. HSC must cite it and position against it.

unique.citation: Hao, Yunkai; Yang, Jian; Ji, Zhigang (2026). Evaluating the Reliability of Cross-Building Load Forecasting Under Distribution Shift and Sensor Missingness. Applied Sciences 16(16), 7984 (published 2026-08-11).
unique.what_it_does: An empirical reliability framework on the HEEW dataset with five-fold cross-building validation (55 main buildings plus 27 extra). It uses a LightGBM residual model against a Lag-1 baseline and tests split-conformal intervals, including variants that scale residuals. 90% intervals cover about 89.0-89.2% for seen buildings and drop to 87.1-87.2% for unseen buildings. Held-out buildings were not used for conformal calibration. PINAW is normalised per building and then averaged. The authors conclude that intervals should be recalibrated before deployment to unseen buildings.
unique.difference_to_HSC: This is the closest building-domain evidence for the problem HSC addresses: pooled calibration under-covers new buildings. It proposes no remedy that uses the new building's own accumulating scores, has no onboarding stages, and reports coverage in aggregate rather than as a per-building distribution or under-covered share.

claimed.citation: Shahid NF. When Average Calibration Fails: Site-Conditional Federated Conformal Risk Control. arXiv preprint (v1 18 Jun 2026, v3 24 Jul 2026); arXiv comment: 'Submitted to the DeCaF Workshop at MICCAI 2026'.
claimed.what_it_does: Uses FeTS-2022 brain-tumour data (1,251 subjects, 20 institutions). A single pooled conformal-risk-control threshold misses the FNR target at 40% of sites. The paper proposes 'risk-curve shrinkage': R_k^shrink(lambda) = w_k*R_k(lambda) + (1-w_k)*R_global(lambda) + corr_k, with w_k = n_k/(n_k+n0). The paper calls this 'the standard empirical Bayes form where n0 acts as prior precision'. n0 is picked by leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis (n0=19 gives 2.7/20 violating sites at a 2.0x stretch). Results are reported per site (violation counts, worst-site FNR).
claimed.difference_to_HSC: The mechanism is essentially HSC's: one pseudo-count weight n/(n+n0) mixes a unit's own calibration curve with a pooled curve (for coverage, a risk curve is 1 minus the score CDF). It also uses leave-one-unit-out tuning and per-unit evaluation. Differences: (1) it is conformal risk control for segmentation FNR, not regression intervals. (2) The units are existing sites with fixed calibration sets; the paper does not address a new site joining with few samples. (3) The prior is the sample-size-weighted global pool, with no similarity (kNN) prior and no stage matching. This fits HSC's own ablation finding that shrinkage, not the prior, is the active ingredient. (4) It adds an ad hoc correction term, the paper calls it 'a heuristic interpolation', there is no guarantee, and n0 is chosen on the same test partitions. It is a workshop preprint. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
claimed.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; arXiv abs page (versions/comments); arXiv HTML full text v3 read via WebFetch (Eq. 2, weight definition, LOSO selection, per-site metrics)

claimed.citation: Mallick S, Tchetgen Tchetgen E, Dobriban E, Lee Y. Generalized Hierarchical Conformal Prediction. arXiv preprint, 16 Aug 2026 (stat.ME).
claimed.what_it_does: Covers prediction for a group after a few (o) of its observations are already collected. Standard hierarchical conformal prediction (HCP) cannot use these, and within-group conformal is uninformative at small o. GHCP restores exchangeability by giving the test group a randomly 'donated' group size. It splits the o observations: floor(o/2) fit a local predictor that is shrunk toward the global one (lambda = floor(o/2)/(|S_train|+floor(o/2))). The rest are held-out scores, pooled with the reference groups' scores in one weighted empirical distribution (Eq. 5). Each reference group gets total weight 1/(|S_cal|+1); the test group gets the same share, with its unobserved part placed at +infinity. Theorem 2.1 proves a finite-sample marginal guarantee. A restricted-donor variant is included. Evaluation uses simulations and the American Community Survey with o in {0,5,10,15,20}.
claimed.difference_to_HSC: Same problem as HSC: a new unit with a few of its own observations, whose own scores are pooled with population scores. GHCP has a finite-sample marginal guarantee; HSC has none. In GHCP the test group's own scores never weigh more than one group's share (1/(K+1)). In HSC the own-score weight n_b/(kappa+n_b+1) grows until the own scores dominate. GHCP has no tuned kappa, no similarity prior and no stage matching. It shrinks the predictor rather than the score CDF, uses unnormalised absolute residuals, and treats o as fixed rather than a growing sequence; there is no time series. Only marginal coverage is reported; I saw no per-group coverage distribution, but the appendix was not fully read. This is the principled counterpart HSC should discuss, and ideally run as a baseline. Not cited in manuscript/references.py; its predecessor Lee et al. 2023 (lee2023hier) is cited.
claimed.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; arXiv abs page; arXiv HTML full text v1 read via WebFetch (Eq. 3 and 5, Theorem 2.1, experimental settings). The last ~106k characters were not read.

claimed.citation: Rafe A, Das S. Socio-Conformal Calibration in Complex Survey Data: Marginal Validity Is Not Enough for Subgroup Reliability. arXiv preprint, 7 May 2026.
claimed.what_it_does: Ordinal conformal prediction on the Pew American Trends Panel (Wave 152; n=4,591; 12 race x education subgroups) over 100 respondent-disjoint splits. It compares split conformal, Mondrian, and a 'regularized Mondrian' comparator: q_g^reg = w_g*q_g + (1-w_g)*q_global, with w_g = n_g/(n_g+lambda) and lambda = 50 fixed. The comparator is motivated by James-Stein shrinkage and 'partial pooling in hierarchical models'. The authors call it 'an empirical comparator, not a theorem-backed contribution'. It reduces threshold instability but gives no decisive fairness gain. The main metric is the survey-weighted subgroup coverage gap.
claimed.difference_to_HSC: Same n/(n+lambda) shrinkage toward a pooled calibration, but applied to quantile thresholds rather than score CDFs. lambda is fixed rather than tuned leave-one-building-out. The groups are static demographic cells, not new units accumulating data; the prior is global with no neighbour prior; the task is classification sets. The neutral or negative result contrasts with HSC's gains and shows the benefit of shrinkage depends on the setting. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
claimed.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; arXiv HTML full text read via WebFetch (Eq. 4, Appendix B on lambda); first surfaced by a WebSearch for empirical-Bayes Mondrian shrinkage

claimed.citation: Lin Z, Trivedi S, Sun J. Conformal Prediction with Temporal Quantile Adjustments. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022), pp. 31017-31030.
claimed.what_it_does: Prediction intervals for cross-sectional time series (for example, patients). The split-conformal quantile is taken over other series' scores at the same time step. TQA adjusts the queried quantile for each series using its own past: TQA-B predicts a rank from an exponentially decayed mean of the series' own residuals; TQA-E uses an ACI-like update delta <- delta + gamma*(err - alpha) on the series' own miscoverages. The paper separates cross-sectional from longitudinal (per-series) coverage. It reports 'tail coverage' = average coverage of the least-covered 10% of series.
claimed.difference_to_HSC: Same evaluation lens: per-unit (longitudinal) coverage and its lower tail, close in spirit to HSC's P10 coverage and share of buildings under 0.85. Also the same structure of population calibration plus the unit's own history. TQA moves the quantile level instead of mixing population and own score distributions with a pseudo-count, and has no similarity prior or onboarding-stage indexing. Its data are health, insurance, COVID, EEG and GEFCom2014 load (days as units). TQA-E is close to HSC's ACI baseline; TQA-B would be a distinct, relevant baseline. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
claimed.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; WebSearch result giving the NeurIPS 2022 proceedings entry and pages; ar5iv full text read via WebFetch (TQA-B/TQA-E definitions, tail-coverage metric, datasets)

claimed.citation: Lin Z, Trivedi S, Sun J. Conformal Prediction Intervals with Temporal Dependence. Transactions on Machine Learning Research (September 2022), per the arXiv comments field.
claimed.what_it_does: Defines cross-sectional and longitudinal validity for time-series regression across a cross-section, and shows distribution-free longitudinal validity is theoretically impossible. CPTD keeps strict cross-sectional validity while improving longitudinal coverage. The test series S_{N+1} is a new unit, exchangeable with the calibration series. Scores are normalised by the series' own past mean absolute residual (CPTD-M) or by a rank-based normaliser (CPTD-R). In CPTD-R a 'prior' rank-percentile of 0.5 'has the same weight as any actual observation'. The interval comes from the cross-sectional quantile of these normalised scores. The metric is mean coverage of the least-covered 10% of series.
claimed.difference_to_HSC: Same evaluation (per-series coverage of new series calibrated on other series), and the impossibility result bounds what HSC can claim per building. The mechanism is related: population calibration of scores normalised by the unit's own history, plus a one-pseudo-observation prior on the rank. HSC instead normalises by mean load and mixes score CDFs with a tuned kappa and a neighbour prior. CPTD is not stage-indexed and its load data is the GEFCom2014 single series with days as units. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
claimed.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; arXiv abs page comments (TMLR Sept 2022); ar5iv full text read via WebFetch (CPTD-M/R, prior weight, tail coverage, datasets)

claimed.citation: Zhang Z, Lu Z, Yang H. The Benefit of Being Bayesian in Online Conformal Prediction. arXiv preprint (v1 Oct 2024, v2 May 2025).
claimed.what_it_does: Online conformal prediction that keeps a belief over the score distribution, regularised by a prior: P_t = lambda_t*P_0 + (1-lambda_t)*empirical distribution of past scores. The paper links this to a Dirichlet-process posterior mean with lambda = alpha/(alpha+n). P_0 is an arbitrary distribution on [0,R], uniform in the main analysis; the theory uses lambda_t = 1/sqrt(t). One belief serves several confidence levels; regret bounds hold in the adversarial case and correct coverage when data are iid.
claimed.difference_to_HSC: The functional form is the same as HSC's mixture F = (kappa*F_prior + #{e_i<=e})/(kappa+n_b+1): a DP-posterior-mean or prior-regularised empirical belief. The difference is the prior: here it is a fixed uninformative distribution, not learned from similar units or matched by stage. There is a single sequence with no population or new-unit structure, and lambda_t follows a theoretical schedule rather than leave-one-building-out tuning. HSC should acknowledge its update as this Bayesian-regularised empirical belief and cite this as the online-conformal precedent. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
claimed.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract (from a title query for 'Bayesian' AND 'conformal'); arXiv HTML v2 read via WebFetch (Eq. 6 belief form, DP link, prior choice)

claimed.citation: Dunn R, Wasserman L, Ramdas A. Distribution-Free Prediction Sets for Two-Layer Hierarchical Models. Journal of the American Statistical Association 2023;118(544):2491-2502.
claimed.what_it_does: Conformal methods for grouped data. CDF pooling is an equal-weight average of the groups' empirical CDFs, with coverage only asymptotic as k grows. Single and repeated subsampling give finite-sample guarantees. Task 1 predicts for a new group. Task 2 predicts a new observation for an existing subject, using a James-Stein shrinkage estimate of that subject's mean in the nonconformity score (finite-sample guarantee from within-subject conformal, non-trivial only if n1 > 1/alpha - 1). The paper states 'supervised conformal methods that borrow strength across subjects to construct prediction sets for an existing subject remain an open problem.'
claimed.difference_to_HSC: HSC's F_prior is a CDF pooling restricted to K neighbour buildings. HSC's problem is Task 2 in a supervised, sequential setting, which is the open problem Dunn et al. name, and that sentence is a good positioning hook. Dunn et al. shrink the location, not the score distribution, and have no time series. Already cited in the manuscript (key dunn2023).
claimed.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; ar5iv full text read via WebFetch (CDF pooling definition, Task 2 shrinkage formula, 'open problem' quote); WebSearch result giving the JASA volume, pages and DOI

claimed.citation: Ding T, Fermanian J-B, Salmon J. Conformal Prediction for Long-Tailed Classification. arXiv preprint (v1 Jul 2025; v3 revised 26 Feb 2026).
claimed.what_it_does: Interp-Q interpolates between class-wise and marginal conformal thresholds: q_y = tau*q_y^CW + (1-tau)*q_hat. A single tau is used for every class, and marginal coverage is at least 1-2*alpha. Fuzzy Classwise CP pools calibration scores across classes with kernel weights on a class embedding (default based on training prevalence), then reconformalises for 1-alpha marginal coverage. The paper also adds a prevalence-adjusted softmax score that targets macro-coverage.
claimed.difference_to_HSC: Its two devices match HSC's two ingredients: interpolating between group-specific and pooled calibration, and similarity-kernel borrowing from other groups. But tau does not depend on a group's sample size, whereas HSC's own-score weight grows with n_b. Classes are not new units accumulating data, the task is classification, and there is no time series or onboarding. Not cited in manuscript/references.py.
claimed.evidence_source: arXiv API abstract; arXiv HTML v3 read via WebFetch (Interp-Q formula, Fuzzy CP weights, guarantees)

claimed.citation: Bersson E, Hoff PD. Optimal Conformal Prediction for Small Areas. Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology 2024;12(5):1464-1488.
claimed.what_it_does: Builds an area-level prediction region for a future observation with guaranteed area-level frequentist coverage. claimed.what_it_does: PCC regresses the offset between per-class and marginal conformal quantiles on label-free descriptors of the classifier head. It also notes that below about 35 test examples per class, worst-class coverage 'becomes unmeasurable before it becomes unachievable'.

claimed.citation: Jeon, Byung-ki (2026). coldstart-conformal-solar: analysis code for auditing cold-start conformal prediction intervals of solar irradiance forecasts at unseen stations (v1.2). Zenodo code record, published 2026-11-06. It accompanies the manuscript "A two-network audit shows when conformal prediction intervals for solar irradiance forecasts remain valid at newly commissioned stations" (Scientific Reports, under review, second revision).
claimed.identifier: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24002627 (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24002626; only one version listed)
claimed.what_it_does: A leave-one-station-out audit of conformal intervals for short-term solar irradiance (GHI) forecasts at a newly commissioned station with no local calibration data. It covers 13 NOAA SURFRAD/SOLRAD stations and 28 PV-Live stations, four base forecasters (including gradient-boosted QR and a multi-quantile NN), horizons from 15 min to 6 h, and nominal levels 80/90/95%. It uses CQR scores max(lo-y, y-hi). It compares eight calibration strategies: raw quantiles; pooled donors; distance-weighted donors; Wasserstein-weighted donors; selected/nearest donors; local-only windows of 1-182 days; a donor+local mixture; delayed-feedback ACI seeded with donor scores; and a full-local-year oracle. It also estimates a 'calibration-budget law' B* (days of local data needed for coverage within 1 pp) and a prospective self-certification rule. In the released code (src/run_cp_matrix.py, src/cp_core.py), the mixture M4_mix gives the donor scores a total mass m (main 150, sensitivity 50 and 400) and each local score weight 1, then takes a weighted CP quantile with test weight 1: Q = inf{q : m*F_donor(q) + #{local <= q} >= (1-alpha)(m + n_local + 1)}. The bundled results digest (NUMBERS.md) shows the mixture beating local-only on Winkler score at budgets of 1, 5 and 21 days, with the gap vanishing by about 91 days. It also shows donor similarity (distance, kt-Wasserstein) not predicting donor suitability: within-fold Spearman rho is about 0, and nearest-donor and pooled give similar shares of stations within 2 pp.
claimed.difference_to_HSC: The mixture formula is algebraically the same as HSC's, with kappa = m. Their m is fixed a priori with a sensitivity grid; it is not chosen by leave-one-unit-out. The domain is solar irradiance at 41 stations, not building or customer load at 842 buildings and 315 clients. Donors are pooled or weighted by geographic or kt distance, not kNN in a load-shape descriptor, and there is no stage-matched prior. Normalisation is clear-sky, not by mean load. The work is not yet peer-reviewed. The record has been public only since 6 Nov 2026, so the two are nearly simultaneous, but the code files carry 1-2 Aug 2026 timestamps. Its finding that similarity weighting does not help matches HSC's null kNN-prior ablation. HSC must cite it and position against it.
claimed.evidence_source: Zenodo record page, Zenodo REST API metadata, and the downloaded code archive (read as text, not executed): research/DESIGN.md, src/cp_core.py, src/run_cp_matrix.py, results/NUMBERS.md, results/revision_r1/NUMBERS_R1.md, revision2/results/NUMBERS_R2.md

claimed.citation: Hao, Yunkai; Yang, Jian; Ji, Zhigang (2026). Evaluating the Reliability of Cross-Building Load Forecasting Under Distribution Shift and Sensor Missingness. Applied Sciences 16(16), 7984 (published 2026-08-11).

It proposes no remedy that uses the new building's own accumulating scores, has no onboarding stages, and reports coverage in aggregate rather than as a per-building distribution or under-covered share.
